newsitem.title: HUNGARY: Hungary's bonds seen stable barring repo cuts.
newsitem.headline: Hungary's bonds seen stable barring repo cuts.

text.p: Hungary's government securities yields will change little this week, dropping only if the central bank cuts its repo rates after recent inflation and household savings figures, analysts said on Monday.
They said yields would move only two or three basis points at most at this weeks government securities auctions and on the secondary market.

But a possible 25-basis-point cut in the National Bank of Hungary's (NBH) repo rates and in the yield of the central bank's one year bond would reduce discount treasury bill yields by about a quarter of a percentage point and government bond yields by a little less than 25 basis points, analysts said.
Hungarian treasury bills have up to one-year maturity, while government bonds range from two years to seven years.
Gabor Pozsgay of Creditanstalt Securities told Reuters he expected a repo rate cut in the near future, probably this week.
"The July inflation figure was very positive, with inflation dropping (month-on-month), which has not happened for a long a time," he said. "We also had very good household savings figures."

July consumer price figures published last week showed that inflation fell 0.1 percent in July after a 1.7 percent month-on-month rise in June, while the year-on-year index was 18.1 percent in July, down from 18.7 percent in June.

NBH preliminary household savings figures published last week showed a 62.9 billion forint rise in July to 2,784.7 billion forints, indicating a return to high levels after a temporary slowdown in the nominal rise in the first quarter.
Traders said neither last week's cut in the forint's devaluation rate, nor a selling wave on the Budapest Stock Exchange (BSE) had affected the government securities market.

The rate of monthly crawling peg devaluation was cut to one percent from 1.1 percent on Friday, but traders said the reduction was small and as it had been pre-announced months before its impact had already been built into prices.

They said capital had not flowed into the government securities markets last week, when the BSE's BUX index fell almost 10 percent due to disappointing first half corporate reports, Wall Street's losses and the dollar's weakening.
Traders said foreign investors' activity on the bond market remained low as foreigners were mainly interested in paper which matures within the next year and supply of which is lacking.
"Foreigners are cautious ahead of the 1998 elections and they are waiting for a decision on next years' devaluation rate," Pozsgay said.
Postabank Securities analyst Attila Torok added share price falls were mainly due to the weakness on Wall Street and in dollar crosses and not domestic economic factors.
"I do not think that (the falls) will influence domestic interest rate levels," he added.

NOTE: The Government Debt Management Agency will auction one-month and three-month T-bills on Tuesday, six-month T-bills on Thursday and twelve-month T-bills on Friday. Wednesday -- the usual day of three-month auctions -- will be a national holiday in Hungary.
